RagShortTexts: Canterbury anchored the spiritual head of the English Church, revered for Saint Thomas.

Variants.Content: Canterbury was the seat of the Archbishop who styled himself Primate of All England, a title that gave the see a claim to supremacy over the English church which Rome repeatedly tested. The archbishop presided over provincial councils, consecrated bishops of the southern province, and held the ancient right to crown the kings. The archbishop could invoke canon law to shield clerks from secular courts, and he could excommunicate men who seized church property. The cathedral priory managed manors, mills, and tithes across Kent, and its revenues swelled with pilgrims at Becket's shrine. Successive kings learned that a quarrel with Canterbury cost them the support of bishops and parish clergy, so the archbishop remained a permanent counterweight to royal ambition.
The Archbishop alone possessed ancient rights to crown English kings, asserting canon law immunities against intrusive royal writs.
